metaDescription: Five budget wood routers under $150 compared on horsepower, collet, speed range and base design, plus what a palm router cannot do that a full-size one can.
expertTake: The WEN RT1460 is the best budget router for most people: a soft-start 6-amp motor, a 12,000 to 30,000 RPM range and a base that is easy to see through. The AVID POWER 6.5-amp is the pick if you want an LED and rack-and-pinion depth, and the TEENO is the aluminum-bodied alternative. The Seesii 21V is the cordless option for trim work. All five are 1/4 inch palm routers, so they are for edges and small joinery, not for big bits.
introParagraphs: A router spins a bit at tens of thousands of RPM to cut edges, grooves and joinery. It is the tool that puts a rounded edge on a tabletop, cuts a hinge mortise and trims laminate flush, and it is more about control and bit quality than horsepower.
This guide explains how speed, collet and base design decide what a compact router can do, which compromises are fine for a homeowner and which cost you accuracy.

products.name: WEN RT1460 6-Amp 1/4 in Variable Speed Laminate Trim Router
products.description:
The WEN RT1460 is a classic laminate trim router. A 6-amp soft-start motor ramps up gradually to prevent the jolt that twists a router in your hand, and the variable speed dial covers 12,000 to 30,000 RPM. The adjustable straight base has 1-5/8 inches of travel and a one-inch scale marked in 1/16 inch steps.

A transparent base lets you see the bit and the line you are following, which matters more than power on a trim router. Speed control matters because bit diameter dictates safe speed: small straight bits run fast, and larger roundover bits need lower speeds. The WEN covers both.

Compared with the AVID POWER, the WEN has soft start and a wider documented speed range. Ownership notes: use sharp carbide bits, make light passes rather than one deep cut and keep your hands clear of the bit. It is the sensible first router. A small trim router like this one is the right tool for hinge mortises, but it cannot plunge into the middle of a board, so use a template and clamp it firmly. Change bits with the router unplugged and tighten the collet nut firmly, but do not bottom the shank, leaving about 1/8 inch of clearance in the collet.
products.bestFor: Beginners who want a controllable trim router for edges and hinges.

products.name: AVID POWER 6.5-Amp 1.25 HP Compact Router with LED
products.description:
The AVID POWER 6.5-amp router has an 800-watt motor, a rack-and-pinion depth system and dual LEDs that light the cutting path. A fixed base keeps the router at a constant depth, and the rack-and-pinion system lets you dial in exact depth with a knob, instead of loosening a clamp and eyeballing.

At 6.5 amps it has slightly more motor current than the WEN RT1460, but no soft start is listed. Bits are included, which helps beginners. The LEDs are a good feature on a trim router, since the bit is small and shadows are common.

Ownership notes: a compact router is best for edges and trim, and 1.25 HP is plenty for those jobs. A lesser-known brand means thin support. If you want the nicest depth adjustment at a low outlay, it is a good choice. If a bit you plan to use has a 1/2 inch shank, this router will not take it, so check the bit catalog before you buy. Keep the dual LEDs clean of dust, since a film of sawdust dims them and makes the cut line harder to follow.
products.bestFor: Woodworkers who want precise depth adjustment and good lighting.

products.name: TEENO 1.25 HP 6.5-Amp Aluminum Compact Router
products.description:
The TEENO is a palm router with a solid aluminum body, an 800-watt copper-wound motor and six speed settings. The maker says it is more durable than plastic models, and a metal body does dissipate heat and resist cracks better. It stands 7.9 inches tall, which is compact for one-handed use.

Compared with the WEN RT1460, the TEENO has a similar 6.5-amp motor, six speeds in place of a dial and a metal body. It is a good choice if you plan to use the router often and want a body that resists drops.

Ownership notes: use the right speed for the bit, keep the base clean and check that the collet nut is tight. For a router that feels sturdy at a low outlay, it is a strong choice. The metal body also gives you a better grip for a base-plate pressure against the work, which keeps the bit at a consistent depth. On aluminum bodies the heat from long sessions moves to the housing, so rest the tool between passes on a long edge.
products.bestFor: Users who want a metal body and six speed steps.

products.name: AVID POWER 5.3-Amp 630 W Compact Trim Router
products.description:
This AVID POWER router has a 5.3-amp, 630-watt motor and runs up to 35,000 RPM, the highest speed in this lineup. Three guide modes help with edge work, and a fixed base keeps the cut depth set. High speed produces a clean finish with small bits, because each cutting edge removes less wood per revolution.

Its motor is weaker than the 6.5-amp AVID and TEENO, so it bogs sooner on deep cuts or hardwood. Compared with the WEN RT1460, it has a higher top speed but no published soft start. It suits trimming laminate, roundovers in pine and light edge work.

Ownership notes: lower speeds suit larger bits, and high speed on a large bit is dangerous. Use light passes, sharp bits and clamp your work. It is the router for trim and small jobs. Bits in the 1/4 inch range, such as a roundover or a chamfer, are the match for this speed, and a 1/2 inch cove bit is not. A router that can reach 35,000 RPM should only run that fast with small, balanced bits, since a large bit at that speed is a hazard.
products.bestFor: Trim and edge work with small bits where a clean finish matters.
pros: 35,000 RPM for a smooth finish with small bits
cons: High speed is risky with large bits

products.name: Seesii 21V Brushless Cordless Palm Router with 2 x 4.0Ah
products.description:
The Seesii is a cordless palm router with a brushless motor, an aluminum base, an LED display and two 4.0Ah batteries. Without a cord you can route trim in place, such as a door jamb or a countertop edge, without dragging a cord across the work.

Cordless routers draw heavy current, so runtime depends on the cut. A 4.0Ah pack is a good size, and two packs let you swap. Compared with the corded WEN RT1460, the Seesii is more convenient but gives up sustained runtime and costs more per unit of power.

Ownership notes: the platform is proprietary, so replacement packs may be hard to find. Brushless motors run cooler and last longer. For trim in place, it is the most convenient choice. Cordless routers also let you route a groove in a finished cabinet without a cord to snag, a real advantage in a kitchen. Allow the bit to stop spinning completely before setting the tool down, because a coasting bit can dig into the work.
products.bestFor: Trim carpenters who want to route in place without a cord.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A router must run slower with larger bits, because the tip of a big bit moves faster. Trim routers run 12,000 to 35,000 RPM, and bits under 1/2 inch run at high speed. Variable speed, like the WEN's dial, lets you match the bit. A single-speed router is risky with big bits. The rule of thumb is higher speeds for small-diameter bits and lower speeds for large ones, so a 1/4 inch straight bit runs happily near the top of the range, and a 1-1/4 inch roundover bit runs near the bottom.

A 1/4-inch collet holds a 1/4-inch shank, the standard on palm routers. A 1/2-inch collet holds bigger bits with less vibration. All five routers here have 1/4-inch collets, so they are for edges and small joinery. Collet quality matters more than size on a budget router: a worn or poorly machined collet lets the bit creep, which leaves chatter marks and can let the bit drop out of the router.

A soft-start motor ramps to speed gradually, avoiding the torque kick that twists the router. The WEN lists it. A router without soft start can jump when you pull the trigger. A soft start also protects the motor and the gearing from the sudden current spike, which extends the life of a small tool.

A rack-and-pinion system, as on the AVID POWER 6.5-amp, lets you set depth precisely. A clamp system is simpler but less precise. Depth accuracy decides whether a hinge mortise fits. Check that the depth knob moves smoothly and holds its setting under vibration, because a depth that creeps by 1/32 inch is the difference between a flush trim and a ridge.

A transparent base and LEDs let you see the bit. A small bit hides behind the motor, so lighting matters. A clear base is only half the answer, because dust blown up by the bit can hide the line. A router with a dust port or a quick blow with compressed air helps.

A corded router has constant power. A cordless router like the Seesii is convenient for trim in place but runs down on deep cuts. A battery router gives up the benefit of constant power for the freedom of the cord, and for edge work that is often a good trade.

specDecoder.meaning: Revolutions per minute of the bit. Trim routers run 12,000 to 35,000.
specDecoder.watchFor: Large bits must run slower. A router that lists only a maximum RPM may not slow down enough for large bits.

specDecoder.meaning: A power rating, usually peak. A 1.25 HP router is about 800 W.
specDecoder.watchFor: Peak ratings can be inflated. A 1.25 HP figure on a budget palm router is a peak rating, and continuous power is lower.

specDecoder.meaning: The chuck that grips the bit shank.
specDecoder.watchFor: A worn collet lets the bit slip.

specDecoder.meaning: A gradual ramp to full speed.
specDecoder.watchFor: It reduces torque kick. A router without soft start can kick on startup, so hold it firmly.

specDecoder.meaning: A fixed base keeps a set depth, a plunge base lowers the bit into the cut.
specDecoder.watchFor: All five here are fixed-base trim routers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Speed and control
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared speed ranges, from the WEN's 12,000 to 30,000 RPM to the AVID's 35,000, and valued soft start. We also checked how speed settings are labeled, because a dial with real RPM numbers is more useful than numbered steps with no values.

howWeEvaluated.title: Depth adjustment
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at rack-and-pinion systems and base visibility. We valued a rack-and-pinion depth knob over a simple clamp, since depth accuracy decides whether hinges and inlays fit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build and platform
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared aluminum bodies, corded and cordless designs and battery packs. A metal base and body, as on the TEENO and the Seesii, received credit for durability.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit contents
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked bits and accessories included. We counted the bits in the box only when they were a useful starter set.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Every router has a live price at or below the cap. We ranked each by how much usable control a homeowner gets for the money.

howToChoose.intro: With small routers the question is not horsepower but what you will use the tool for.
The router prices here are close, so the ranking follows features rather than power.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: Constant power and no battery. The WEN, AVID and TEENO are corded.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: Convenient but limited. The Seesii is cordless.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded for shop work and cordless for trim in place.

howToChoose.intro: How you set depth decides how accurate your cuts are.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A fixed base, a transparent base plate and a speed range up to 30,000 RPM. Use a flush trim bit with a bearing.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The WEN RT1460 is designed for laminate trimming, and the AVID POWER 5.3-Amp's 35,000 RPM gives a clean edge.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You route weekly or need larger bits. A 1/2 inch collet router with plunge base is more versatile.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You route edges occasionally. The WEN or AVID is enough.

maintenance.why: Dust makes the bit slip. Dust packed in the collet also scores the bit shank, so wipe the shank before you insert it.
A dull bit burns wood and overloads the motor. Carbide bits cost a few dollars each and last for hours, but a bit that has lost its edge pushes the wood and chatters.
A loose base gives uneven depth. A base that has any play makes depth drift, so tighten the base screws until there is no wobble.
Dust clogs the motor. Compressed air through the vents clears the packed dust before it reaches the bearings.

faq.a: A small one-handed router with a 1/4-inch collet, used for edges and trim. A palm router is also called a trim router or a laminate trimmer, and it is the standard size for a first router.

faq.q: Do I need a plunge router?
faq.a: For mortises and grooves in the middle of a board, yes. Fixed-base trim routers cannot plunge. A plunge router lets you lower the spinning bit into the wood, which is what you need for mortises and stopped grooves.

faq.q: What bit should I start with?
faq.a: A roundover bit and a flush trim bit cover most jobs. Start with a roundover bit and a flush-trim bit, which together handle most edge work in a first year of woodworking.

faq.q: Why does my router burn wood?
faq.a: A dull bit, a slow feed or too high a speed. Replace the bit and move steadily. Feed the router against the rotation of the bit, which means moving left to right along an outside edge, to keep it from running away.
Against the bit rotation, usually from left to right along an outside edge. Cutting a deep profile in one pass overloads a small router, so take two or three shallow passes of about 1/8 inch each.

faq.q: Can I use a trim router for big bits?
faq.a: No. Use a larger router. A 1/4 inch router is limited to smaller bits, and a 1/2 inch router is the next step if you want cove or raised-panel bits.
